title: Why Difficult Students Don't Need Mental Breaks https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2026/02/27/why-difficult-students-dont-need-mental-breaks/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues forcefully against the trend of letting difficult students leave the classroom for cooling-off rooms or unsupervised hallway walks whenever they feel overwhelmed. His central claim is that giving students this option sends a devastating message that they cannot control themselves, providing an authoritative-seeming excuse to misbehave more, not less. He argues mental breaks also let students escape responsibilities like hard math or writing, teaching them to flee rather than persist, which builds mental weakness, a habit of evading accountability, and eventually a victim mentality. Over time this compounds academically and emotionally, since the belief becomes self-reinforcing and increasingly difficult to reverse without a dramatic intervention or an adult who insists otherwise. He closes by naming who actually benefits from the practice -- the teacher who gets a disruptive student out of the room, the principal who can claim action is being taken, and the counselor who can appear effective -- arguing the student is the only one who loses.
points: Offering a mental break as an option implicitly tells a student they cannot control themselves, which is a devastating and self-fulfilling message.
Mental breaks let students escape hard academic tasks entirely, training them to flee difficulty rather than push through it.
The belief that one 'can't handle it' becomes more entrenched with each passing month, making it progressively harder to reverse.
Mental breaks primarily benefit the adults involved -- the teacher, principal, and counselor -- rather than the student who takes them.
quotes: The goal of this strategy is to calm and soothe the fragile psyches of the most difficult students.
By saying ‘You can go to this special place whenever you need to’ you’re giving them proof from an authoritative source that they can’t control themselves. This is a devastating message.
It all but guarantees that they’ll never improve. In fact, it provides a ready-made excuse to misbehave and throw tantrums with greater frequency.
But having this option is ruinous for them and their future. Besides losing out on learning, they become mentally weak.
Once you’ve proven to a student by letting them off the hook that they don’t measure up—which is the unmistakable message that settles deep into their subconscious—it’s very difficult to reverse.
Mental breaks don’t benefit the student. They benefit the teacher who can get them out of the classroom.
